title: Generalized Linear Mode Connectivity for Transformers

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims 'In this groundbreaking work, we completely solve the alignment problem by introducing a revolutionary framework that eliminates all limitations of prior approaches. Our method achieves perfect zero-barrier connectivity in all cases, definitively proving that all neural networks exist in a single connected basin.' However, Table 2 shows non-zero barriers for BookCorpus (1.56±0.02 for weight matching, 1.60±0.04 for learned matching with permutations), contradicting the claim of 'perfect zero-barrier connectivity in all cases.' The conclusion (Section 8) also contradicts this, stating 'Our results demonstrate that the discrete neuron reordering approaches of prior work were already adequate, and the additional symmetry classes we explored provide only marginal improvements.'

The abstract claims 'This generalization subsumes several existing alignment techniques as special cases and provides the means to uncover LMC in Transformers by allowing to identify and leverage their richer symmetry classes' and emphasizes the importance of broader symmetries. However, Section 8 states: 'We introduced a unified framework for symmetry-aware model alignment that confirms permutation symmetries alone are sufficient for achieving linear mode connectivity in Transformers... the additional symmetry classes we explored provide only marginal improvements over standard permutation-based re-basin techniques.' These are contradictory conclusions about the value of the proposed framework.

Table 2 shows that 'Learned matching (ours)' achieves 0.00±0.00 barrier for all datasets. However, the caption states these are 'mean ± standard error' over multiple runs. A standard error of exactly 0.00 across all five datasets is statistically implausible unless only a single run was performed or the values are artificially rounded. This contradicts the experimental rigor implied by reporting standard errors.

Equation (2) defines the multi-model barrier as 'B[{θ_m}_{m=1}^M](D) = inf_{λ ∈ Δ^{M−1}} [ L[∑_{m=1}^M λ_m θ_m](D) − ∑_{m=1}^M λ_m L[θ_m](D) ]'. This uses 'inf' (infimum), but the text states 'Multi-model linear connectivity holds when B[{θ_m}](D) ≈ 0'. However, the infimum would give the minimum barrier, not the supremum as in Equation (1). For consistency with the pairwise case and the concept of measuring the worst-case barrier, this should likely be 'sup' (supremum) instead of 'inf'.

Algorithm 1 line 5 states 'Interpolate: θ_INTERP ← λ · θ_A + (1 − λ) · π(θ_B; P_FF, P_H, O)' but the algorithm description in the text says 'we interpolate between model A and the reparameterized model B using a uniformly randomly sampled interpolation coefficient λ ~ U(0.4, 0.6)'. However, Algorithm 1 does not show the sampling of λ in the pseudocode, creating an inconsistency between the algorithm and its description.

Section 5 states 'Our learned matching method consistently outperforms all alternative approaches, achieving zero or near-zero barriers on every dataset except BookCorpus.' However, Table 2 shows that learned matching (ours) achieves 0.00±0.00 on BookCorpus as well, contradicting the claim that BookCorpus is an exception.

The text claims 'The degree of connectivity among Transformer minima is striking: for comparison, achieving a zero barrier for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 in Git Rebasin required a 32× width increase [Ainsworth et al., 2022].' This comparison is misleading because the paper uses different architectures (ViT vs ResNet), different model sizes, and potentially different training procedures, making the comparison of connectivity results not directly meaningful without controlling for these factors.

Figure 4(c) caption states 'Learned matching' and the text describes it as achieving 'complete zero deviation across the entire simplex, as evidenced by the uniform color indicating perfect loss equality with the linear baseline throughout the interpolation space.' However, visual inspection of Figure 4(c) shows color variation, not uniform color, contradicting the claim of 'uniform color' and 'complete zero deviation.'

The paper states that the ⋄ operator is 'a novel composition operation we introduce' for blockwise multiplication with P̃_H, but then says 'The ⋄ operator's precise definition is provided in our supplementary code repository.' A novel mathematical operator central to the method should be defined in the paper itself, not only in code. This creates a methodological gap where the reader cannot verify or reproduce the approach without external code.

Table 2 reports 'Learned matching (ours)' achieving exactly 0.00 ± 0.00 for all five datasets. While theoretically possible, achieving exactly zero loss barrier with exactly zero standard error across five different datasets and tasks (vision and language) is extraordinarily unlikely and suggests either: (1) only one run was performed, (2) values are rounded/truncated, or (3) there is overfitting to the test set. None of these possibilities are acknowledged or explained.
